questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B)

📌 Rule / Concept: Modal Verb “Must” in Passive Voice (Modal + be + V³)

When a sentence contains a modal verb such as must, the passive structure follows the fixed pattern: Modal + be + V³

The modal does not change. The object becomes the subject, and the main verb changes into its past participle (V³).

Active Structure: Subject + must + V¹ + Object

Passive Structure: Object + must + be + V³

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

In modal passive constructions, always insert “be” after the modal. Never omit “be.” Do not change the modal unless required. The fixed structure “modal + be + V³” is one of the most frequently tested voice patterns in SSC examinations.

department insisted that the innovative concept for the upcoming digital campaign was
actually their and had been conceptualized during the previous quarter.
No Error
options_hi: While the marketing team successfully defended their strategy during the meeting, the creative
department insisted that the innovative concept for the upcoming digital campaign was

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C).

Replace “their” with “theirs”

Rule / Concept: Possessive Adjectives vs. Possessive Pronouns

Possessive Adjectives (my, our, your, his, her, its, their) must always be followed by a noun because they function as modifiers (e.g., their strategy). Possessive Pronouns (mine, ours, yours, his, hers, its, theirs) stand alone and replace the "Possessive Adjective + Noun" structure to avoid repetition. They never take a noun after them.

NOTE: POSSESSIVE PRONOUN = POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE + NOUN

Example: yours = your + dog (noun)

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, there is no noun following the word "their." Since the sentence is referring to "the creative department's concept" without repeating the word "concept," a possessive pronoun is required. "Their" is an adjective and cannot stand alone; "theirs" is the correct pronoun.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

-The Noun Check: Always look at what follows the word. If there is a noun (e.g., their house), use the adjective. If there is a verb or a full stop (e.g., is theirs.), use the pronoun.

-The "s" Factor: Except for "mine," most possessive pronouns end in "s" (ours, yours, hers, theirs).

-Avoid the Apostrophe: Never use an apostrophe with possessive pronouns (theirs, NOT their's).

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: Beyond the jagged peaks of the Himalayan mountain range
was situated several ancient monasteries that had remained
untouched by modern civilization for over five centuries.
No Error
options_hi: Beyond the jagged peaks of the Himalayan mountain range
was situated several ancient monasteries that had remained
untouched by modern civilization for over five centuries.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “was situated” with “were situated”. 📌 Rule / Concept: Full Inversion with Place Adverbials

When a sentence begins with a Prepositional Phrase of Place (e.g., Beyond the hills, Under the tree, At the end of the street), and the verb is a verb of position or motion (e.g., be, stand, lie, sit, situated, located), Full Inversion occurs.

In Full Inversion, the entire verb comes before the subject. Crucially, the verb must agree with the subject that follows it, not the noun in the prepositional phrase.

💢 Application to the Given Question

...was situated several ancient monasteries...

In this sentence, the subject is "several ancient monasteries" (plural). The phrase at the beginning, "Beyond the jagged peaks of the Himalayan mountain range," is merely a place adverbial. Because the subject is plural, the verb must be "were situated" instead of the singular "was situated."

Corrected Sentence

Beyond the jagged peaks of the Himalayan mountain range were situated several ancient monasteries that had remained untouched by modern civilization for over five centuries.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅: Under the table lies a sleeping cat. (Singular subject)

Example 2 ✅: Among the trees were many colorful birds. (Plural subject)

Example 3 ✅: At the top of the hill stands an old lighthouse. (Singular subject)

My father has said to me, "Honesty is the best policy."
options_en: My father has told me that honesty was the best policy.
My father had said to me that honesty is the best policy.
My father told me that honesty is the best policy.
My father has told me that honesty is the best policy.
options_hi: My father has told me that honesty was the best policy.
My father had said to me that honesty is the best policy.
My father told me that honesty is the best policy.
My father has told me that honesty is the best policy.
questions.solution_en:
The correct answer is Option D: My father has told me that honesty is the best policy.

Key Points

  • Reporting Verb in Present Perfect: The reporting verb "has said to" is in the Present Perfect tense.

    • Rule: If the reporting verb is in the Present (e.g., says), Present Perfect (e.g., has said), or Future (e.g., will say), the tense of the verb in the reported speech does not change.

  • Reporting Verb Change: Just like "said to" changes to "told," the phrase "has said to" changes to "has told" when followed by an object ("me").

  • Universal Truth/Proverb: The statement "Honesty is the best policy" is a universal truth or a proverb.

    • Rule: Even if the reporting verb were in the past tense (e.g., said), the tense of a universal truth or proverb typically remains in the Simple Present.

  • Eliminating Incorrect Options:

    • Option A is incorrect because it changes the tense of the proverb to the past ("was").

    • Option C is incorrect because it changes the reporting verb from Present Perfect ("has told") to Simple Past ("told").

    • Option B is incorrect because "had said to me" should be changed to the more appropriate "had told me" in indirect speech.

questions.q_en: Although the path was steep and dangerous, __________ the trekkers refused to turn back.
questions.q_hi: Although the path was steep and dangerous, __________ the trekkers refused to turn back.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option D

👉 The blank should be filled with “yet”.

📌 Rule / Concept: The "Although... yet" Pair

In formal grammar, Although and Though are correlative conjunctions. They introduce a contrast and must be followed by a specific "partner" word or punctuation to complete the sentence structure.

The Rule: Although/Though must be paired with yet or a comma ( , ).

The Error: Using but with Although is a redundancy error because both words perform the same function (showing contrast).

Why "But" is Wrong:

If you use "but," you are effectively saying: "Even though it was dangerous, BUT they went." This is like using two steering wheels for one car; it is redundant and grammatically "crowded."

✅ Correct Sentence: Although the path was steep and dangerous, yet the trekkers refused to turn back.

questions.solution_en:

Replace “three-fourth” with “three-fourths”

Rule / Concept: Pluralizing Fractions

In English grammar, when expressing a fraction in words, the denominator (the second part) follows a specific rule based on the numerator (the first part):

If the numerator is 1: The denominator remains singular.

Example: One-third, One-fourth, One-fifth.

If the numerator is greater than 1: The denominator must be in its plural form (add an 's').

Example: Two-thirds, Three-fourths, Five-sixths.

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the numerator is "three" (which is greater than one). Therefore, the denominator "fourth" must be pluralized to match. It should be "three-fourths."

Corrected Sentence - Because of multiple server issues, he could solve only three-fourths of the questions in the exam

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 - One-fourth of the cake is gone. (Numerator is 1, so 'fourth' is singular)

Example 2 - Three-fourths of the cake are gone. (Numerator is 3, so 'fourths' is plural)

Example 3 -Two-thirds of the work is complete. (Numerator is 2, so 'thirds' is plural).

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: After the devastating fire at the library,
there was little or nothing left of
the historical manuscripts and records.
No Error
options_hi: After the devastating fire at the library,
there was little or nothing left of
the historical manuscripts and records.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (D) No Error.

Rule / Concept: Correlative Adverbial Phrases

  • Little or nothing: (Negative + Negative) Uses "or" to connect two similar ideas of "hardly any" and "none."

  • Little if anything: (Negative + Hypothetical) Uses "if" to suggest that even if something exists, it is very little.

LITTLE IF ANYTHING :- ( POSITIVE , meaning = a little)

➢ LITTLE OR NOTHING:- (NEGATIVE , meaning = little)

Application to the Given Question

"...there was little or nothing left of the historical manuscripts..."

In this sentence, the phrase "little or nothing" is used accurately to describe the state of the manuscripts after the fire. It conveys that almost nothing—and potentially absolutely nothing—remained. Since the phrase follows the mandatory "or + nothing" pairing, there is no grammatical error.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1: The shipwreck contained little or nothing of value. ✅

Example 2: There is little if anything to be done about the situation now. ✅

Example 3: He has little or nothing to do with the day-to-day operations. ✅

Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1: He understands little or anything about the subject. (Correct: little if anything) ❌

Wrong example 2: There was little if nothing left in the fridge. (Correct: little or nothing) ❌

questions.q_en: Identify the sentence in which the word “since” is used as a preposition.
questions.q_hi: Identify the sentence in which the word “since” is used as a preposition.
options_en: Since the roads were flooded, the buses could not operate normally.
I have not spoken to her since Monday.
Since you insist, I will reconsider the proposal.
The company has expanded rapidly since it changed its management.
options_hi: Since the roads were flooded, the buses could not operate normally.
I have not spoken to her since Monday.
Since you insist, I will reconsider the proposal.
The company has expanded rapidly since it changed its management.
questions.solution_en:
Answer: B) I have not spoken to her since Monday.

Explanation: A preposition is followed by a noun or pronoun and shows its relationship with another word.

In option B, “since” is followed by the noun “Monday.”

since Monday

Therefore, “since” functions as a preposition.

Why other options are incorrect:

A) “since” joins two clauses: Since the roads were flooded + the buses could not operate normally. Hence, it is a conjunction.

C) “since” introduces the clause “you insist.” Therefore, it is a conjunction.

D) “since” connects two clauses: The company has expanded rapidly + it changed its management. Hence, it is a conjunction.
